query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent protective oxide layer forms and persists during exposure above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than developing unstable surface oxides that crack or spall? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted differences, the applicable exposure and material-state boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsifying observation.

generation.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys, the nature of the protective oxide layer formed above 900 °C is controlled by which element (Si, Mn, or Al) predominantly diffuses to the surface and reacts with oxygen. Specifically, when X = Al or Si, the slower cation diffusion and stronger bonding promote the formation of slow-growing, adherent oxides (Al2O3 or SiO2) that heal defects and resist spallation, whereas when X = Mn, the faster diffusion and tendency to form volatile or poorly adherent oxides result in unstable, cracking oxide scales.
generation.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX alloys (with X being Si, Mn, or Al) produced as single- or multiphase metallic solid solutions with identical overall compositions except for the substituent element.
generation.intervention: Expose the alloys to high-temperature (above 900 °C) oxidative or corrosive environments.
generation.conditions: Samples are maintained at temperatures above 900 °C under controlled oxidizing conditions (or corrosive atmospheres) for a prolonged duration (e.g., 100 hours).
generation.structural_mediator: The microstructure and coherence of the surface oxide scale, governed by elemental segregation kinetics and oxide phase stability.
generation.mechanism: Differential elemental diffusion: Al and Si, when present, diffuse more slowly and form thermodynamically stable oxides with low growth rates and high adherence, whereas Mn diffuses more rapidly and forms oxides that are prone to cracking and spallation due to higher diffusivity and volatile oxide species.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys with Al or Si will develop a coherent, protective oxide scale that limits further oxidation, while alloys with Mn will display discontinuous, cracked, and spalled oxide layers leading to faster degradation.
generation.baseline: Comparative evaluation among CrFeCoNiX alloys that are identical in all respects except the identity of X (Al, Si, or Mn).
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies for high-entropy alloys that are in a single- or multiphase solid-solution state and exposed to temperatures above 900 °C in oxidizing/corrosive environments; different oxidation mechanisms may prevail at lower temperatures or under non-oxidative conditions.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative impact of multiphase microstructures on the diffusion kinetics of the different alloying elements and oxide adherence properties requires further in situ high-temperature characterization.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize three sets of CrFeCoNiX alloys where X is alternately Al, Si, or Mn, ensuring identical processing routes to obtain comparable single- or multiphase solid solutions. Expose these samples in a controlled furnace at temperatures above 900 °C in an oxidative atmosphere for a fixed duration (e.g., 100 hours). Perform post-exposure analysis comparing oxide scale continuity, adhesion (using scratch or pull-off tests), phase identification by XRD, and microstructural imaging via SEM.
measurements: Mass gain measurements (TGA) to assess overall oxidation rates
XRD to identify oxide phases and their coherence
SEM imaging to evaluate oxide scale morphology and presence of cracks or spallation
Adhesion tests (e.g., scratch tests) to quantify the bonding quality of the oxide scales
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the CrFeCoNiMn alloy exhibits oxide scale characteristics (continuity, adhesion, and phase stability) comparable to those observed in the CrFeCoNiAl and CrFeCoNiSi alloys, then the hypothesis that element-specific diffusion governs the formation of protective vs. unstable oxides is falsified.

Previous studies have indicated that Cr2O3 is the sole stable phase in the Cr-O system, known for its compact structure and superior oxidation resistance []. However, it is noteworthy that Cr2O3 was not detected in the in situ XRD analysis conducted for this study. One of the most promising applications of FeNiCoCrMoAl-based high-entropy alloy is the fabrication of protective coatings. In this work, gas-atomized powder of FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 composition was deposited via high-velocity oxygen fuel spraying. It was shown that in-flight oxidation of the powder influences the coating’s phase composition and properties. Powder oxidation and phase transformations were studied under HVOF deposition, and during continuous heating and prolonged isothermal annealing at 800 °C. Optical and scanning electron microscopy observation, energy dispersive X-ray analysis, X-ray diffraction analysis, thermogravimetric analysis, differential thermal analysis, and microhardness tests were used for study. In a gas-atomized state, the powder consisted of BCC supersaturated solid solution. The high rate of heating and cooling and high oxygen concentration during spraying led to oxidation development prior to decomposition of the supersaturated solid solution. Depleted Al layers of BCC transferred to the FCC phase. These scales can function as barriers, retardation the diffusion of corrosive species and offering a modicum of protection against additional corrosion. The alloying elements (Fe, Co, Ni, Mn, and Cu) could help form stable oxide scales in the coating, which has contributed to mitigate the corrosion susceptibility. In addition, the continuous exposure to high temperatures and corrosive environments may result in the development of a stronger passive oxide layer on the surface of SS-304, furthermore preventing corrosion. Even if initially compromised, the coating may moderately obstruct the diffusion of corrosive ions, deceleration the rate of corrosion over time. Although, the corrosion typically progresses to an equilibrium state over time, where the initial quick corrosion may retard down as the system acclimates to the corrosive circumstances.

AbstractFour different high-entropy spinel oxide ferrite (HESO) electrode materials containing 5–6 distinct metals were synthesized by a simple, rapid combustion synthesis process and evaluated as conversion anode materials in lithium half-cells. All showed markedly superior electrochemical performance compared to conventional spinel ferrites such as Fe3O4 and MgFe2O4, having capacities that could be maintained above 600 mAh g–1 for 150 cycles, in most cases. X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) results on pristine, discharged, and charged electrodes show that Fe, Co, Ni, and Cu are reduced to the elemental state during the first discharge (lithiation), while Mn is only slightly reduced. Upon recharge (delithiation), Fe is reoxidized to an average oxidation state of about 2.6+, while Co, Ni, and Cu are not reoxidized. The ability of Fe to be oxidized past 2+ accounts for the high capacities observed in these materials, while the presence of metallic elements after the initial lithiation provides an electronically conductive network that aids in charge transfer.
